Here are two small words that confuse a lot of learners: used to. They can mean three different things. First, I used to, plus a verb, is about the past. I used to live in Rio means I lived there before, but not now. Second, I'm used to, plus i-n-g, means that something is normal for me. I'm used to working late, so it isn't hard. Third, I'm getting used to is the process: something is new, and it's becoming normal, step by step. I'm getting used to my new job. One more thing. After be used to and get used to, we use the i-n-g form, or a noun. So say, I'm used to speaking English. Don't say, I'm used to speak English. And if something is still strange for you, don't worry. You'll get used to it.

Hi Vanessa, it's Marcos, from Toronto. It's been three months, so I wanted to tell you how it's going. The first few weeks were hard. I wasn't used to the cold at all, and I felt really self-conscious at work, because everyone speaks so fast. But gradually, things are changing. I'm getting used to the accent, and now I'm used to taking the subway at seven, in the snow! The thing I still can't get used to is dinner at six in the evening. That's far too early for a Brazilian. Anyway, here's my advice for you: don't hold back in your meetings. You'll get used to it faster than you think. Talk soon!

First, something new feels awkward, and I hold back. Then I try it again, even if I feel self-conscious. After that, I gradually get used to it. Next, I'm used to it, and it becomes second nature. In the end, I look back and see that I've come a long way.
